newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Airline pressure builds for joint fare hike.
newsitem.headline: Airline pressure builds for joint fare hike.

text.p: Pressure built from European airlines on Wednesday for a joint decision by global carriers to raise passenger ticket prices to compensate for a 30 per cent hike in jet fuel prices this year.

As officials from many of the more than 250 member companies of the International Air Transport Association (IATA) met in Geneva to discuss a concerted increase, the Finnish airline Finnair indicated it wanted a rise.

The Finnair signal followed an announcement by the joint Scandinavian airline SAS on Tuesday that it was putting up prices for travellers by two per cent and for cargo by five per cent with effect from next weekend.

But an IATA spokesman said that the closed-door meeting at the body's Geneva offices was expected to look at the situation airline by airline and was unlikely to come up with a decision before late on Friday.

In the highly competitive air travel industry, emerging from the recession of the early 1990s which left IATA members with a collective loss of more than $15 billion, many companies are reluctant to take action that might drive away business.

Many Asian carriers are known to be wary of putting up prices, although some have added surcharges to their cargo rates to make up for the rising cost of fuel -- which accounts for around 10 per cent of operating costs for most airlines.

A joint move would mean no company could cash in by keeping its prices down to attract passengers from its rivals -- but airline analysts say even if a collective decision were taken some carriers could be tempted to break ranks.

Finnair spokesman Usko Maatta told Reuters in Helsinki the company, which has a strong network of routes in Europe and Asia, was waiting for the outcome of the Geneva discussions -- IATA's first emergency meeting on fares since the 1991 Gulf War.
"There would be a need to up prices, but we are waiting to see if the meeting comes up with a coordinated move," he said.

IATA's Director-General Pierre Jeanniot told the global body's annual general meeting in Geneva last week that after a good year in 1995 its members collectively were heading for record profits of $5,5 billion this year.

But this forecast was half a billion dollars down on a prediction he had made in April at a time when the fuel price rises were only just beginning to bite. Fuel cost was a key element in the revision, Jeanniot told reporters.
IATA airlines account for around 98 per cent of international scheduled flights.

In the past week, several have returned figures for the first half of the year showing how bottom lines have been hit by fuel costs, including British Airways, which reported a 2.1 percent drop in operating profits compared to a year ago.

BA said strong traffic growth and greater productivity would have boosted profits by 10.5 percent had it not been for an extra 51 million pounds ($84 million) spent on its fuel bills together with the impact of a threatened pilots strike in July.

Airlines paid an average worldwide price last year of 65.2 U.S. cents a gallon (4.5 litres). But the price soared to 77.5 cents in September after the United States fired 27 cruise missiles against Iraq as a warning to Baghdad to comply with Gulf War ceasefire resolutions.

IATA sources said decisions open to officials at the Geneva meeting included raising fares across the board or on a select number of routes, or simply to levy surcharges on some or all of their routes.
